title: Blood Supply & the Blood–Brain Barrier
summary: How the brain gets its blood and protects itself chemically.

lessons.title: Carotid & Vertebrobasilar Systems

levels.kid:
Your brain is very hungry. It needs lots of blood to bring it air and food, all day and all night.

Blood gets to your brain through four big pipes in your neck. Two pipes are in the front of your neck. You can feel them beating if you touch the side of your neck. They are called the carotid arteries.

Two more pipes run up the back of your neck, hidden inside little holes in your neck bones. They are called the vertebral arteries. They join together into one pipe at the bottom of your brain.

The front pipes feed most of the big thinking brain. The back pipes feed the parts that help you balance, breathe and stay awake.
levels.hs:
The brain is only about 2% of body weight but uses about 15–20% of the blood the heart pumps. Blood reaches it through **two systems**:

**1. The carotid (anterior) system**
- The **common carotid arteries** run up each side of the neck. The right one comes from the brachiocephalic trunk; the left comes straight off the aortic arch.
- At about the level of the upper thyroid cartilage, each splits into an **external carotid** (face, scalp) and an **internal carotid artery (ICA)**.
- The ICA enters the skull and divides into the **anterior cerebral artery (ACA)** and **middle cerebral artery (MCA)**, which feed most of the front and sides of the brain. It also gives off the **ophthalmic artery** to the eye.

**2. The vertebrobasilar (posterior) system**
- The **vertebral arteries** come off the subclavian arteries, climb through holes in the neck vertebrae, and enter the skull through the foramen magnum.
- They join to form the **basilar artery** along the front of the brainstem.
- The basilar ends by splitting into the two **posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs)**. Along the way, branches feed the brainstem and cerebellum.

**Why it matters:** blockage in the carotid system often causes weakness, numbness or language trouble. Blockage in the posterior system causes dizziness, double vision, trouble swallowing, imbalance and even coma, because the brainstem controls consciousness and breathing.
levels.college:
**Anterior circulation.** The common carotid bifurcates around C3–C4. The ICA has **no branches in the neck**, a key way to tell it from the ECA on angiography. Intracranial course (Bouthillier segments): **C1 cervical, C2 petrous, C3 lacerum, C4 cavernous, C5 clinoid, C6 ophthalmic, C7 communicating**. The cavernous and supraclinoid ICA form the **carotid siphon**. Branches above the cavernous sinus, in order: **ophthalmic artery**, **posterior communicating artery (PComm)**, **anterior choroidal artery**, then terminal bifurcation into **ACA** and **MCA**. The anterior circulation carries roughly 70–80% of cerebral blood flow.

**Posterior circulation.** Each **vertebral artery** (segments V1–V4) arises from the subclavian, enters the transverse foramen usually at **C6**, ascends through C6–C1, loops behind the atlas (V3), pierces the dura and enters through the foramen magnum (V4). Intracranially each gives the **posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)** and contributes to the **anterior spinal artery**. The vertebrals join at the **pontomedullary junction** to form the **basilar artery**, which gives the **anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA)** (often with the labyrinthine artery), **pontine perforators**, the **superior cerebellar arteries (SCA)**, and terminates in the **PCAs** at the midbrain.

**Clinical syndromes:**
- **Carotid stenosis**: atherosclerosis at the bifurcation causes emboli: transient ischemic attacks, **amaurosis fugax** (transient monocular blindness via the ophthalmic artery), and MCA strokes. Symptomatic high-grade stenosis is treated with **carotid endarterectomy** or stenting.
- **Vertebral dissection**: after neck trauma or sometimes minor strain; neck or occipital pain followed by posterior circulation stroke.
- **Subclavian steal**: proximal subclavian stenosis reverses flow down the vertebral artery when the arm is exercised, causing dizziness or syncope.
- **Posterior circulation symptoms**: vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia, crossed signs (cranial nerve deficit on one side, body deficit on the other).
levels.phd:
**Embryology explains variants.** Early in development the ICA supplies most of the brain, including the posterior territory through what becomes the PComm; the basilar forms from fusion of paired longitudinal neural arteries fed by transient carotid–basilar anastomoses (trigeminal, otic, hypoglossal and proatlantal). Persistence gives adult variants: the **persistent trigeminal artery** (most common, linking cavernous ICA to basilar) matters during transsphenoidal or cavernous sinus surgery. A **fetal PCA** (PCA filled mainly from the ICA via a large PComm with hypoplastic P1) means a carotid occlusion can cause occipital infarction. **Vertebral dominance** (often left) and a vertebral artery ending in PICA are common.

**Hemodynamics and autoregulation.** Cerebral blood flow is held relatively constant across a range of perfusion pressures via myogenic, metabolic and neurogenic mechanisms. CO2 is the most potent acute regulator: hypercapnia dilates arterioles and raises flow. In chronic hypertension the autoregulatory curve shifts right, so rapid blood pressure lowering can cause hypoperfusion.

**Atherosclerosis distribution.** Plaque favors the carotid bulb, where flow separation and low, oscillatory wall shear stress activate endothelial pro-inflammatory programs (NF-κB, VCAM-1), while laminar high shear induces protective KLF2/KLF4 expression.

**Plaque vulnerability** beyond percent stenosis: intraplaque hemorrhage, a lipid-rich necrotic core and thin fibrous cap on vessel wall MRI predict stroke risk and may refine who benefits from revascularization in asymptomatic stenosis, where modern best medical therapy has lowered event rates and trials continue to weigh benefit.

**Measuring stenosis.** NASCET measures narrowing relative to the normal distal ICA, ECST relative to the estimated bulb diameter, so the same lesion gives different numbers. The benefit of endarterectomy in symptomatic 70–99% (NASCET) stenosis is greatest when surgery is done within about two weeks of the event.

**Posterior circulation physiology.** Brainstem perforators are end arteries with minimal collateral, explaining why small occlusions cause dense deficits.
levels.expert:
**Recognizing posterior circulation stroke** is a known diagnostic weakness: isolated dizziness is often labeled peripheral vertigo. Use the **HINTS exam** (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) in acute continuous vertigo: a normal head impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation points to a central (stroke) cause, and early MRI can miss small posterior strokes. Look for crossed signs, dysarthria, ataxia and Horner's syndrome.

**Basilar artery occlusion** may present with fluctuating consciousness, quadriparesis, ophthalmoplegia or locked-in syndrome. It is often preceded by stuttering symptoms and carries high mortality without recanalization. Endovascular thrombectomy improves outcomes in selected patients and the treatment window is often treated as longer than in the anterior circulation.

**Carotid disease in practice.** Symptomatic stenosis (TIA or minor stroke in the territory within the past months) with high-grade narrowing benefits from endarterectomy, ideally within two weeks. Stenting is an alternative for hostile necks (prior radiation or surgery, high bifurcation) and carries a higher periprocedural stroke risk, especially in older patients, while endarterectomy carries more myocardial infarction and cranial nerve injury risk (hypoglossal, marginal mandibular, recurrent laryngeal). **Cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome** after revascularization (headache, seizures, hemorrhage) is prevented by strict blood pressure control.

**Dissection.** Cervical artery dissection is a major cause of stroke in young adults. Clues: neck pain, headache, **partial Horner's syndrome** (ptosis and miosis without anhidrosis, since the sympathetic fibers for facial sweating travel with the ECA), pulsatile tinnitus or lower cranial nerve palsies. Antithrombotic therapy (antiplatelet or anticoagulant) is used.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Proximal ICA control in the neck is a classic safety step before clipping a giant or ophthalmic segment aneurysm. Balloon test occlusion assesses whether a patient tolerates ICA sacrifice. Bypass surgery (for example STA–MCA) supplies flow in moyamoya disease or when a vessel must be sacrificed.

keyPoints: Two systems: carotid (anterior) and vertebrobasilar (posterior).
ICA has no neck branches; intracranially: ophthalmic, PComm, anterior choroidal, then ACA + MCA.
Vertebral arteries rise through transverse foramina (usually from C6), give PICA, and join to form the basilar.
Basilar gives AICA, pontine perforators, SCA, then splits into the PCAs.
Carotid stenosis → TIA, amaurosis fugax, MCA stroke; treated with endarterectomy when symptomatic and severe.
Posterior circulation stroke: vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia, crossed signs.

examples.src: A 68-year-old describes a curtain coming down over one eye for five minutes, then clearing.
examples.tr: Amaurosis fugax: an embolus from ipsilateral carotid disease into the ophthalmic artery. Urgent carotid imaging.

examples.src: A 35-year-old with sudden neck pain after a sports injury, then vertigo and unsteadiness.
examples.tr: Vertebral artery dissection causing posterior circulation ischemia.

test.q: Which arteries form the anterior (carotid) circulation inside the skull?
test.explain: The internal carotids enter the skull and feed most of the cerebral hemispheres.

test.q: The left common carotid artery usually arises from the:
test.explain: On the left, the common carotid comes straight off the arch; on the right it comes from the brachiocephalic trunk.

test.q: Which branch does the ICA give off in the neck?
test.explain: The cervical ICA classically has no branches; the ophthalmic arises intracranially.

test.q: The two vertebral arteries join to form the:
test.explain: They merge at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery.

test.q: The vertebral arteries usually enter the transverse foramina at which level?
test.explain: Most commonly at C6, then they ascend through C6–C1.

test.q: The basilar artery ends by dividing into the:
test.explain: The basilar bifurcates at the midbrain into the two PCAs.

test.q: Transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax) most often comes from emboli into the:
test.explain: Carotid plaque emboli travel to the ophthalmic artery, the first major intracranial ICA branch.

test.q: Which symptom combination points most to the posterior circulation?
test.explain: Brainstem and cerebellar ischemia cause vertigo, double vision, ataxia, dysarthria and dysphagia.

test.q: Subclavian steal causes symptoms because:
choices: Flow reverses down the vertebral artery to supply the arm
test.explain: Proximal subclavian stenosis makes the arm 'steal' blood backward down the ipsilateral vertebral artery.

test.q: Partial Horner's syndrome with neck pain in a young adult suggests:
test.explain: Dissection damages the sympathetic plexus on the ICA wall; neck pain plus ptosis and miosis is a classic clue.

test.q: Name the surgery that removes plaque from the carotid artery.
test.explain: Carotid endarterectomy removes plaque in symptomatic high-grade stenosis to prevent stroke.

test.q: The largest branch of the vertebral artery, supplying the lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum, is the ___ (abbreviation).
test.explain: PICA (posterior inferior cerebellar artery) arises from the intracranial vertebral artery; its occlusion is linked to lateral medullary syndrome.

test.q: The S-shaped curve of the cavernous and supraclinoid ICA is called the carotid ___.
test.explain: The carotid siphon is visible on lateral angiograms.

kidTest.q: Why does your brain need blood?
choices: To bring it air and food
kidTest.explain: Blood carries oxygen and sugar that brain cells need.

kidTest.q: How many big pipes bring blood to your brain?
kidTest.explain: Two carotids in front and two vertebrals in back.

kidTest.q: Where can you feel the carotid artery beating?
kidTest.explain: Put two fingers gently on the side of your neck to feel it.

kidTest.q: Where do the vertebral arteries run?
choices: Up the back of the neck through bone holes
kidTest.explain: They travel through little holes in your neck bones.

kidTest.q: The two back pipes join into one pipe called the ___ artery.
kidTest.explain: The vertebral arteries join into the basilar artery.

kidTest.q: What do the back pipes feed?
choices: Parts for balance, breathing and staying awake
kidTest.explain: They supply the brainstem and cerebellum.

advancedTest.q: Ptosis and miosis WITHOUT facial anhidrosis in carotid dissection happen because:
choices: Sudomotor fibers to the face travel with the external carotid
advancedTest.explain: Sympathetic fibers on the ICA serve the eye and Müller's muscle; facial sweat fibers follow the ECA, so they're spared.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a fetal PCA on the right undergoes right ICA occlusion. Which territory is unexpectedly at risk?
advancedTest.explain: With a fetal PCA, the right PCA territory depends on the right ICA via the PComm.

advancedTest.q: Acute continuous vertigo with nystagmus. Which HINTS finding is reassuring for a PERIPHERAL cause?
advancedTest.explain: A corrective saccade on head impulse indicates a peripheral vestibular lesion; a normal head impulse in acute vertigo is worrying for stroke.

advancedTest.q: Compared with carotid endarterectomy, carotid stenting has:
choices: Higher periprocedural stroke risk, especially in older patients
advancedTest.explain: Trials (e.g. CREST) found more periprocedural strokes with stenting and more MIs and cranial nerve palsies with endarterectomy.

lessons.title: The Circle of Willis

levels.kid:
At the bottom of your brain, the big blood pipes join together in a ring. It is called the circle of Willis, named after a doctor from long ago.

Think of it like a roundabout for cars. Cars can come in from different roads and still get where they need to go. If one road is blocked, cars can drive around the circle and take another road.

The circle works the same way for blood. If one pipe gets a little blocked, blood can flow around the ring from the other pipes, so the brain still gets fed.

Sometimes a pipe in the circle has a weak spot that puffs out like a little balloon. Brain doctors can fix that with tiny clips or coils.
levels.hs:
The **circle of Willis** is a ring of connected arteries at the base of the brain, around the optic chiasm and pituitary stalk. It links the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems.

**The parts of the ring:**
- The two **anterior cerebral arteries (ACAs)**, joined in front by the short **anterior communicating artery (AComm)**.
- The two **internal carotid arteries (ICAs)** at the sides.
- The two **posterior communicating arteries (PComms)**, which connect each ICA to the posterior cerebral artery.
- The two **posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs)**, coming from the top of the basilar artery.

The **middle cerebral arteries (MCAs)** branch off the ICAs here too, but they are not part of the ring itself.

**Why have a circle?** It provides **backup routes (collateral flow)**. If one carotid narrows slowly, blood can cross over through the communicating arteries. But many people don't have a complete circle: some segments are tiny or missing, so the backup doesn't always work.

**Aneurysms:** the circle's branch points have weak spots where **berry (saccular) aneurysms** form. If one bursts, blood floods the subarachnoid space, which is a **subarachnoid hemorrhage**. Patients often describe the "worst headache of my life," coming on in seconds (a thunderclap headache). Common spots: the AComm, the junction of the ICA and PComm, and the MCA bifurcation.

Neurosurgeons treat aneurysms by **clipping** them through a craniotomy or by **coiling** them from inside the artery using a catheter.
levels.college:
**Components:** A1 segments of both ACAs, the AComm, the supraclinoid ICAs, both PComms and the P1 segments of both PCAs. The circle lies in the suprasellar and interpeduncular cisterns, encircling the optic chiasm, infundibulum, tuber cinereum and mammillary bodies.

**Perforating arteries** arise from the circle and its proximal branches to supply deep structures: the **recurrent artery of Heubner** (from distal A1 or proximal A2) to the head of the caudate and anterior limb of the internal capsule; **lenticulostriate arteries** (from M1) to the basal ganglia and internal capsule; **thalamoperforators** (from P1 and PComm) to the thalamus. These are end arteries, so their occlusion causes lacunar infarcts.

**Variants are the rule:** a complete textbook circle is found in well under half of people. Common variants include a hypoplastic PComm, a hypoplastic or absent A1, and a **fetal PCA** (the PCA fed mainly by the ICA through a large PComm).

**Aneurysms.** About 85% of saccular aneurysms are in the anterior circulation. Most common sites: **AComm**, **ICA–PComm junction**, **MCA bifurcation**, then the basilar tip. Risk factors: smoking, hypertension, family history, **autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease**, connective tissue disorders (Ehlers–Danlos type IV), and coarctation of the aorta.

**Localizing clues:** a **PComm aneurysm** can compress CN III, producing a palsy with a **dilated pupil** ("down and out" eye with ptosis), because pupillary parasympathetic fibers run on the nerve's surface. A pupil-sparing CN III palsy is more typical of microvascular (diabetic) ischemia, which affects the core.

**SAH complications:** rebleeding (highest in the first hours to day), **hydrocephalus**, **delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm** (peaking roughly days 4–14), hyponatremia, seizures and cardiac stress. Nimodipine improves outcome after aneurysmal SAH.
levels.phd:
**Hemodynamics of aneurysm formation.** Saccular aneurysms arise at bifurcation apices where the flow stream impinges. High wall shear stress and its spatial gradient at the apex trigger endothelial dysfunction, matrix metalloproteinase activity, loss of the internal elastic lamina and medial thinning. Once a bleb forms, low and oscillatory wall shear inside the sac drives inflammatory remodeling (macrophage infiltration, NF-κB signaling) that weakens the wall. Two phenotypes are proposed: high-flow, high-shear driven mural cell-mediated growth, and low-flow inflammatory degeneration. This duality explains why both low and high wall shear stress have been associated with rupture in different computational fluid dynamics studies.

**Genetics.** Familial aneurysms cluster, and GWAS have identified risk loci (for example near CDKN2A/B, SOX17, EDNRA). Smoking and hypertension are the largest modifiable risks.

**Natural history and risk scoring.** Most unruptured aneurysms never bleed. The **PHASES** score (Population, Hypertension, Age, Size, Earlier SAH, Site) estimates five-year rupture risk; posterior circulation and PComm aneurysms carry higher risk than equivalent cavernous ICA aneurysms, which rarely cause SAH because they are extradural. Irregular shape, daughter sacs and growth on surveillance increase risk.

**Collateral capacity of the circle.** Collateral flow depends on vessel diameter (Poiseuille: flow scales with the fourth power of radius), so a hypoplastic PComm adds little. Primary collaterals (circle of Willis) act fast; secondary collaterals (leptomeningeal anastomoses and ophthalmic reversal) are recruited when primary ones fail. Collateral status strongly predicts infarct growth and outcome in acute stroke thrombectomy.

**Delayed cerebral ischemia** is no longer thought to be explained by large-vessel vasospasm alone: microthrombosis, cortical spreading depolarizations, microcirculatory dysfunction and early brain injury all contribute, explaining why drugs that reversed angiographic spasm did not improve outcomes.
levels.expert:
**Aneurysmal SAH: the first hours.** Sudden severe headache reaching peak within about a minute. Non-contrast CT is highly sensitive within the first six hours; if CT is negative later, LP for xanthochromia or CTA. Grade with **Hunt and Hess** or **WFNS** and the modified **Fisher** scale (blood amount predicts vasospasm). Priorities: airway, blood pressure control to reduce rebleeding until the aneurysm is secured, reversal of anticoagulation, EVD for hydrocephalus, and nimodipine.

**Secure early.** Rebleeding carries high mortality, so the aneurysm is secured within about 24–72 hours. **ISAT** showed better one-year independent survival with **endovascular coiling** than clipping for aneurysms suitable for both, at the cost of more retreatment. Modern choices weigh anatomy and age: wide-necked, MCA bifurcation aneurysms and those with mass effect or a large hematoma often favor **microsurgical clipping** (a hematoma can be evacuated in the same operation); posterior circulation (especially basilar tip) aneurysms often favor endovascular treatment. Flow diverters and intrasaccular devices expand endovascular options for unruptured aneurysms.

**Clipping principles:** proximal control (sometimes in the neck), wide arachnoid dissection, temporary clipping with neuroprotective strategy, sparing perforators (especially at the AComm, where hypothalamic and forniceal perforators matter, and Heubner's artery), and confirming occlusion and branch patency with **indocyanine green videoangiography** or Doppler. Watch for a clip causing ICA or branch stenosis, monitored with MEPs.

**Vasospasm window.** Daily neuro exams and transcranial Doppler; a new deficit prompts CT perfusion or angiography, maintaining euvolemia and inducing hypertension, with intra-arterial vasodilator or angioplasty if refractory. Prophylactic hypervolemia is no longer advised.

**AComm complex** anatomy is the most variable in the brain: duplicated AComm, fenestrations and a dominant A1 change both approach side and clip strategy.

keyPoints: Circle of Willis: ACAs (A1) + AComm + ICAs + PComms + PCAs (P1).
It allows collateral flow between carotid and vertebrobasilar systems, but a complete circle is found in less than half of people.
Most saccular aneurysms are anterior: AComm, ICA–PComm junction, MCA bifurcation.
PComm aneurysm compresses CN III → ptosis, down-and-out eye, dilated pupil.
SAH: thunderclap headache; complications include rebleeding, hydrocephalus and delayed ischemia from vasospasm.
Treatment: clipping (craniotomy) or endovascular coiling.

examples.src: Sudden 'worst headache of my life' while lifting weights, then neck stiffness and vomiting.
examples.tr: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise: CT head immediately.

examples.src: New right ptosis, the right eye down and out, and a large right pupil, with headache.
examples.tr: Compressive CN III palsy: urgent CTA for a right PComm aneurysm.

test.q: The circle of Willis connects which two arterial systems?
test.explain: It links the internal carotids with the basilar/PCA system.

test.q: Which artery is NOT part of the ring itself?
test.explain: The MCA branches off the ICA but is not a segment of the ring.

test.q: The anterior communicating artery connects:
test.explain: The AComm is a short link between the two anterior cerebral arteries.

test.q: What is the most common site of a saccular aneurysm?
test.explain: The AComm complex is the most common site, followed closely by the ICA–PComm junction.

test.q: A PComm aneurysm classically compresses which nerve?
test.explain: The oculomotor nerve runs beside the PComm.

test.q: Why does a compressive CN III palsy often dilate the pupil?
choices: The pupil fibers are in CN VI
The pupil fibers run on the outside of the nerve
test.explain: Parasympathetic pupillary fibers lie superficially, so external compression hits them first.

test.q: The classic headache of subarachnoid hemorrhage is described as:
choices: Only on one side behind the eye with tearing
Sudden, worst ever, peaking in seconds to a minute
test.explain: A thunderclap onset is the hallmark.

test.q: Which condition increases the risk of berry aneurysms?
test.explain: ADPKD is a classic association, along with smoking, hypertension and family history.

test.q: Delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm after SAH typically peaks:
test.explain: Vasospasm risk rises after day 3 and peaks within the first two weeks.

test.q: Which drug class member is given after aneurysmal SAH to improve outcome?
test.explain: Nimodipine, a calcium channel blocker, improves neurological outcome after aneurysmal SAH.

test.q: Name the endovascular treatment that fills an aneurysm with platinum wire.
test.explain: Coils packed into the sac promote thrombosis and seal it off from circulation.

test.q: The arteries arising from M1 that supply the basal ganglia are the ___ arteries.
test.explain: Lenticulostriate perforators are end arteries; their occlusion causes lacunar strokes.

test.q: A PCA fed mainly by the ICA through a large PComm is called a ___ PCA.
test.explain: A fetal PCA is a common variant that changes which territory a carotid occlusion affects.

kidTest.q: What is the circle of Willis?
choices: A ring of blood pipes under the brain
kidTest.explain: It is a ring of arteries at the bottom of the brain.

kidTest.q: The circle is like a:
kidTest.explain: Blood can go around it like cars on a roundabout.

kidTest.q: Why is the circle helpful?
choices: If one pipe is blocked, blood can go another way
kidTest.explain: It gives backup routes.

kidTest.q: A weak spot that puffs out on a pipe looks like a:
kidTest.explain: That bubble is called an aneurysm.

kidTest.q: Doctors can fix a weak spot with tiny clips or ___.
kidTest.explain: Clips pinch it closed from outside; coils fill it from inside.

advancedTest.q: In ISAT, for ruptured aneurysms suitable for either treatment, coiling compared with clipping showed:
choices: Better one-year independent survival but more retreatment
advancedTest.explain: Coiling had better one-year independence; late retreatment and rebleeding were somewhat more common.

advancedTest.q: Why did drugs that reversed angiographic vasospasm fail to improve outcomes after SAH?
choices: The drugs could not reach the brain
Delayed ischemia is multifactorial (microthrombi, spreading depolarizations, early brain injury)
advancedTest.explain: Large-vessel spasm is only part of delayed cerebral ischemia; e.g. clazosentan reduced spasm without improving functional outcome.

advancedTest.q: Which unruptured aneurysm location carries the LOWEST risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage?
advancedTest.explain: Cavernous ICA aneurysms are extradural; they can cause cranial neuropathies or carotid-cavernous fistula but rarely SAH.

advancedTest.q: By Poiseuille's law, halving the radius of a communicating artery reduces its flow (all else equal) to about:
advancedTest.explain: Flow scales with radius to the fourth power: (1/2)^4 = 1/16.

lessons.title: Arterial Territories

levels.kid:
Each blood pipe in your brain feeds its own neighborhood, like each garden hose waters its own part of the garden.

One pipe feeds the part that moves your legs. Another feeds the parts that move your face and arms and help you talk. A pipe at the back feeds the part that lets you see.

If a pipe gets blocked, its garden patch stops getting water, and that part of the brain stops working. That is called a stroke.

So doctors can play detective! If someone suddenly can't move one arm or can't talk, the doctor can guess which pipe is blocked, and fix it fast. Fast help saves brain.
levels.hs:
Each major artery feeds a specific region, or **territory**. Because each brain region has a job, a blocked artery produces a predictable set of symptoms. Remember: the left brain controls the right side of the body, and vice versa.

**Anterior cerebral artery (ACA):** inner (medial) surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, where the **leg** area lives. Stroke → weakness and numbness of the opposite **leg** more than the arm, plus personality changes or loss of motivation.

**Middle cerebral artery (MCA):** the big outer surface of the brain. Stroke → weakness and numbness of the opposite **face and arm** more than the leg, the eyes looking toward the side of the stroke, and loss of half the visual field. If on the **left** (usually the language side): **aphasia**, trouble speaking or understanding. If on the **right**: **neglect**, ignoring the left side of the world.

**Posterior cerebral artery (PCA):** the occipital lobe (vision) and parts of the thalamus and temporal lobe. Stroke → loss of the opposite half of vision in both eyes (**homonymous hemianopia**), sometimes with the center of vision spared.

**Brainstem and cerebellum** (vertebral, basilar, PICA, AICA, SCA): dizziness, double vision, trouble swallowing, slurred speech, clumsiness, and "crossed" signs.

**Tiny deep arteries** cause small **lacunar strokes**, for example pure weakness of one side.

**BE FAST** helps spot stroke: Balance, Eyes, Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech trouble, Time to call emergency services.
levels.college:
**ACA**: medial frontal and parietal cortex (paracentral lobule), anterior corpus callosum. Deficits: contralateral leg > arm weakness and sensory loss, **abulia**, urinary incontinence (medial frontal micturition center), transcortical motor aphasia (dominant), and alien hand features (callosal).

**MCA**: lateral frontal, parietal and superior temporal cortex, insula, and via **lenticulostriates** the basal ganglia and internal capsule. A full **M1** occlusion causes contralateral face/arm > leg weakness and sensory loss, **gaze deviation toward the lesion**, homonymous hemianopia (optic radiations), plus **global aphasia** (dominant) or **neglect and anosognosia** (non-dominant). **Superior division** → face/arm weakness and Broca's (expressive) aphasia. **Inferior division** → Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia, superior quadrantanopia, little weakness.

**Anterior choroidal**: posterior limb of the internal capsule, optic tract, LGN, medial temporal lobe → hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, hemianopia.

**PCA**: occipital lobe, inferomedial temporal lobe, thalamus (thalamoperforators, thalamogeniculate). Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with **macular sparing** (MCA collaterals reach the occipital pole); dominant PCA + splenium → **alexia without agraphia**; thalamic infarct → contralateral sensory loss and sometimes later **thalamic pain** (Dejerine–Roussy).

**Posterior fossa:**
- **PICA / vertebral** → **lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome**: ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, contralateral body pain and temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner's, dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), vertigo, ipsilateral ataxia.
- **AICA** → lateral pontine syndrome: similar, plus ipsilateral facial weakness and hearing loss (labyrinthine artery).
- **Anterior spinal / vertebral paramedian** → **medial medullary syndrome**: contralateral hemiparesis and proprioception loss, ipsilateral tongue weakness.
- **Basilar** → bilateral signs, coma, or **locked-in syndrome** (ventral pons).

**Watershed (border zone) infarcts** occur between territories, e.g. ACA–MCA, during hypotension: proximal arm and leg weakness ("man in a barrel").
levels.phd:
**Territory maps are probabilistic, not fixed.** Classic templates show average distributions, but individual territories vary considerably, especially at borders. Variants (fetal PCA, dominant A1 supplying both ACAs, hypoplastic segments) shift territories, and collateral recruitment after occlusion changes the eventual infarct. Lesion-symptom mapping across large stroke cohorts has refined which deficits arise from which voxels, moving beyond artery-based classification.

**Penumbra concept.** After occlusion, a core of irreversibly injured tissue (flow below the threshold for membrane failure, ion pump failure, anoxic depolarization) is surrounded by a **penumbra**: tissue below the threshold for electrical function but above that for structural integrity, salvageable if reperfused. Its persistence depends on collaterals; "fast progressors" with poor collaterals lose penumbra in an hour, "slow progressors" keep it for many hours. This biology underlies imaging-based selection for late thrombectomy (perfusion mismatch, as in DAWN and DEFUSE-3).

**Lacunar mechanisms.** Small deep infarcts arise from lipohyalinosis and microatheroma of perforators, mainly driven by hypertension. Classic lacunar syndromes: pure motor (posterior limb of internal capsule or basis pontis), pure sensory (VPL thalamus), ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria–clumsy hand and sensorimotor stroke. They predict cerebral small vessel disease burden (white matter hyperintensities, microbleeds).

**Brainstem localization as a logic problem.** Medial brainstem syndromes involve the **4 Ms** (motor pathway, medial lemniscus, medial longitudinal fasciculus, motor nuclei of III, IV, VI, XII), lateral syndromes the **4 Ss** (spinothalamic, sensory nucleus of V, sympathetic pathway, spinocerebellar), with cranial nerve level indicating height (rule of 4). This framework predicts Wallenberg and Weber syndromes from first principles.

**Watershed physiology.** Border zones are the most distal irrigation fields with lowest perfusion pressure; internal (deep) border-zone infarcts in a row-of-beads pattern strongly associate with hemodynamic compromise from carotid occlusion.
levels.expert:
**Time is brain.** In a large-vessel occlusion, roughly 1.9 million neurons are lost per minute (Saver's estimate). Pre-hospital scales (for example RACE, VAN) identify likely LVO for direct transport to thrombectomy centers.

**Hyperacute pathway.** NIHSS on arrival, non-contrast CT to exclude hemorrhage, CTA head and neck for LVO, and CT perfusion when selecting late-window patients. **Intravenous thrombolysis** (alteplase or tenecteplase) is given in eligible patients within 4.5 hours of last known well. **Mechanical thrombectomy** is standard for anterior LVO (ICA, M1, and many proximal M2) within 6 hours and up to 24 hours with favorable imaging; large-core trials (e.g. SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT) extended benefit to bigger infarcts, and basilar occlusion trials (ATTENTION, BAOCHE) showed benefit.

**Pattern recognition traps:**
- **Gaze deviation** toward the lesion is a cortical sign of a large MCA stroke; gaze deviation away from the lesion suggests a seizure focus or a pontine lesion.
- **Isolated aphasia** with no weakness can be an inferior division MCA stroke, easily mistaken for confusion or psychiatric illness.
- **Bilateral leg weakness** can be bilateral ACA infarcts from a single dominant A1, mimicking spinal cord disease.
- **Top-of-the-basilar** syndrome causes visual loss, abnormal eye movements, somnolence and behavioral changes from bilateral thalamic and occipital infarcts; an **artery of Percheron** occlusion gives bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts with sudden coma.
- **Wallenberg** often comes from vertebral occlusion, not PICA alone; aspiration risk is high, so assess swallowing first.

**Malignant MCA infarction.** Massive MCA infarcts swell over two to five days. **Decompressive hemicraniectomy** within 48 hours in patients up to 60 reduces mortality substantially (DESTINY, DECIMAL, HAMLET), with many survivors moderately disabled; it is an informed choice with the family. **Cerebellar infarcts** that swell compress the fourth ventricle and brainstem; suboccipital decompression is lifesaving.

keyPoints: ACA: leg > arm, contralateral; abulia, incontinence.
MCA: face/arm > leg, gaze toward lesion, hemianopia; dominant → aphasia, non-dominant → neglect.
PCA: contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.
PICA/vertebral → lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome with crossed sensory loss and Horner's.
Lenticulostriate occlusion → lacunar stroke (e.g. pure motor hemiparesis from the internal capsule).
Watershed infarcts occur between territories during low blood pressure.

examples.src: Right face and arm weakness with inability to speak fluently, eyes deviated to the left.
examples.tr: Left MCA (superior division or M1) stroke.

examples.src: Sudden vertigo, hoarseness, left Horner's, left face and right body pain/temperature loss.
examples.tr: Left lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from left vertebral/PICA occlusion.

examples.src: Left leg weakness much worse than the arm, with apathy.

lessons.title: Venous Drainage

levels.kid:
Blood goes into your brain through arteries. After the brain uses the air and food in the blood, the used blood has to leave. It leaves through veins.

Some veins run on the outside of the brain, like little streams on a hill. Some veins are deep in the middle of the brain. All these little streams flow into bigger rivers inside the tough brain blanket. Those rivers are called sinuses.

The rivers flow down to two big veins in your neck, and then back to your heart.

If a vein gets clogged, the used blood can't leave. Then the brain gets puffy and can bleed. Doctors can give medicine that helps the clog go away.
levels.hs:
After brain tissue takes oxygen and glucose from arterial blood, the used (deoxygenated) blood drains through **veins**. Brain veins have two special features: they have **no valves**, and they drain into **dural venous sinuses** rather than directly into neck veins.

**Two systems:**
- **Superficial veins** run on the brain surface in the subarachnoid space. Most drain upward into the **superior sagittal sinus**; others drain into the transverse or cavernous sinuses. Some named ones: the **vein of Trolard** (to the superior sagittal sinus) and the **vein of Labbé** (to the transverse sinus).
- **Deep veins** drain the deep structures (thalamus, basal ganglia, deep white matter). They join into the **internal cerebral veins**, which form the **great cerebral vein of Galen**, which drains into the **straight sinus**.

All sinuses eventually reach the **sigmoid sinuses** and the **internal jugular veins**.

**Bridging veins** cross from the brain surface to the sinuses through the subdural region. They tear in head injuries, causing **subdural hematomas**.

**Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST)**: a clot in a sinus or vein. Blood can't drain, so pressure rises, causing headache, blurred vision, seizures and sometimes bleeding. It is more common in pregnancy and after childbirth, with dehydration, some hormone medicines, and clotting disorders. It's treated with blood thinners.

Venous strokes don't match arterial territories, which is a clue for doctors reading scans.
levels.college:
**Superficial (cortical) system.** Superior cerebral veins drain the dorsolateral and medial hemisphere into the **superior sagittal sinus (SSS)**, entering against the direction of sinus flow. The **superficial middle cerebral (Sylvian) vein** drains into the **sphenoparietal or cavernous sinus**. Two anastomotic veins connect these: the **superior anastomotic vein of Trolard** (Sylvian vein to SSS) and the **inferior anastomotic vein of Labbé** (Sylvian vein to transverse sinus).

**Deep system.** The **septal vein** and **thalamostriate vein** join at the foramen of Monro (the **venous angle**) to form the **internal cerebral veins**, which run in the roof of the third ventricle (velum interpositum). They join the **basal veins of Rosenthal** to form the **vein of Galen**, which joins the inferior sagittal sinus to become the **straight sinus**.

**Brainstem and cerebellum** drain via petrosal veins (to the superior petrosal sinus) and vermian and precentral cerebellar veins to the Galenic system.

**Outflow.** Sinuses → sigmoid → **internal jugular veins**; additional outflow through vertebral venous plexuses, especially when upright, and through emissary veins.

**Venous infarction** differs from arterial infarction: it crosses arterial boundaries, often involves subcortical regions and is frequently **hemorrhagic** because of high venous pressure. Deep venous thrombosis (internal cerebral veins, straight sinus) causes **bilateral thalamic** edema with confusion or coma.

**CVST** diagnosis: CT venography or MR venography; the **cord sign** (hyperdense thrombosed cortical vein) and **dense triangle/empty delta sign**. Treatment: anticoagulation even with hemorrhage, address the cause, manage seizures and ICP; endovascular therapy for deterioration.

**Neurosurgical significance:** preserving bridging veins and the veins of Labbé and Trolard during retraction and dural opening, since venous injury can cause delayed swelling, hemorrhage and deficits.
levels.phd:
**Venous physiology is underappreciated.** The brain holds a large share of its blood volume in veins, which makes venous outflow a key determinant of intracranial pressure. Cortical veins are not passive tubes: at their entry into the sinuses, **bridging veins** pass through a cuff region where wall structure changes, acting like a **Starling resistor**. When ICP rises, these segments partly collapse, keeping cortical venous pressure slightly above ICP and preserving outflow. This coupling explains why venous pressure tracks ICP and why cerebral perfusion pressure is better defined as MAP minus the higher of ICP or venous pressure.

**Posture and outflow.** Supine, outflow is mostly via the internal jugular veins; upright, the jugulars partially collapse and the vertebral venous plexus takes over. Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome has prompted study of how loss of gravitational unloading shifts venous congestion.

**Thrombosis biology.** CVST risk reflects Virchow's triad: hypercoagulable states (pregnancy, estrogens, thrombophilias such as factor V Leiden or prothrombin mutation, antiphospholipid syndrome, malignancy), stasis (dehydration) and local infection or injury. Vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT), described in 2021, presented predominantly as CVST with antibodies against platelet factor 4, a striking example of immune-driven venous thrombosis.

**Venous hypertension syndromes.** Dural AV fistulas with cortical venous reflux, and pial AVMs, arterialize veins and cause congestive edema, dementia-like syndromes and hemorrhage. **Vein of Galen malformations** are direct arteriovenous shunts into a persisting embryonic median prosencephalic vein, presenting in neonates with high-output heart failure.

**Developmental venous anomalies** (venous angiomas) are the most common vascular malformation: a caput medusae of deep medullary veins drains normal brain. They are usually harmless but often coexist with cavernous malformations, and resecting a DVA can cause venous infarction.
levels.expert:
**Venous anatomy shapes every craniotomy.** Before operating, review venous phase angiography or venography to map the SSS, dominant transverse sinus, veins of Labbé and Trolard, and large bridging veins. A subtemporal approach that sacrifices a dominant **vein of Labbé** can cause temporal venous infarction with hemorrhage, seizures and, on the dominant side, aphasia. Interhemispheric approaches are planned between bridging veins; a large one may be dissected free along the cortex or the approach shifted, rather than coagulated. Retractor pressure on venous outflow causes congestion, so modern technique minimizes fixed retraction.

**Deep venous system in surgery.** The internal cerebral veins and vein of Galen are among the most dangerous structures to injure; bilateral occlusion can cause thalamic infarction and coma. In pineal region surgery (infratentorial supracerebellar approach), the tumor sits beneath the Galenic complex. Transcallosal approaches to the third ventricle work through or around the foramen of Monro, sometimes requiring care with the septal and thalamostriate veins.

**CVST at the bedside.** Suspect it in any headache with papilledema, focal seizures, or hemorrhages that are bilateral, parasagittal or don't fit an artery, especially postpartum, with estrogen therapy, dehydration, ear or sinus infections (mastoiditis → sigmoid sinus thrombosis) or known malignancy. Isolated headache can be the only symptom. Anticoagulate; consider endovascular thrombectomy if the patient deteriorates despite treatment, and decompressive craniectomy for large venous infarcts with herniation. Monitor vision in those with raised pressure. Recurrence risk guides how long treatment continues.

**Subdural surgery.** Acute SDH usually comes from bridging vein tears; evacuation through a large craniotomy allows control of the bleeding vein. Look for and coagulate the culprit vein near the sinus without injuring the sinus itself.

**Carotid–cavernous fistula** (traumatic, high-flow) arterializes the ophthalmic veins: pulsatile proptosis, chemosis, bruit and ophthalmoplegia; endovascular closure is standard.

keyPoints: Brain veins are valveless and drain into dural venous sinuses, then the internal jugular veins.
Superficial veins → mostly superior sagittal sinus; vein of Trolard (to SSS) and vein of Labbé (to transverse sinus).
Deep veins → internal cerebral veins + basal veins of Rosenthal → vein of Galen → straight sinus.
Bridging veins tearing cause subdural hematomas.
Venous infarcts cross arterial territories and are often hemorrhagic.
CVST: headache, papilledema, seizures; treated with anticoagulation even with hemorrhage.

examples.src: Postpartum woman with headache for three days, then a focal seizure; CT shows bilateral parasagittal hemorrhages.
examples.tr: Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis with venous hemorrhagic infarcts.

examples.src: Child with ear infection, then headache and swelling behind the ear, with double vision.
examples.tr: Mastoiditis with sigmoid/transverse sinus thrombosis and raised pressure (CN VI palsy).

test.q: Which feature is true of cerebral veins?
test.explain: Without valves, flow can reverse, which allows infection to spread from the face to the sinuses.

test.q: Venous infarcts differ from arterial infarcts because they:

test.explain: Pregnancy and the postpartum period are classic hypercoagulable states.

test.q: Deep venous system thrombosis typically injures the:
test.explain: Internal cerebral veins and straight sinus drain the thalami; clot causes bilateral thalamic edema.

test.q: The main treatment for CVST is:
test.explain: Anticoagulation prevents clot propagation and helps recanalization, even if hemorrhage is present.

test.q: The internal cerebral veins form at the foramen of Monro from the thalamostriate vein and the:
test.explain: The septal and thalamostriate veins meet at the venous angle.

test.explain: Most superior cerebral veins enter the superior sagittal sinus.

test.explain: Contrast outlines the sinus wall around a non-enhancing clot.

kidTest.q: What are veins for?
kidTest.explain: Veins carry used blood away from the brain.

kidTest.q: What are the big rivers inside the brain blanket called?
kidTest.explain: Dural sinuses collect blood from brain veins.

kidTest.q: Where does the used blood go after the sinuses?
choices: Down veins in the neck back to the heart
kidTest.explain: It goes through the neck veins to the heart.

kidTest.q: What happens if a brain vein gets clogged?
choices: Used blood can't leave and the brain gets puffy
kidTest.explain: Blood backs up, causing swelling and sometimes bleeding.

kidTest.q: Blood goes into the brain through arteries and leaves through ___.
kidTest.explain: Arteries bring blood in; veins take it out.

advancedTest.q: Bridging veins behaving as Starling resistors implies that:
choices: Venous outflow pressure falls below ICP
ICP has no effect on veins
Cortical venous pressure is kept slightly above ICP
advancedTest.explain: Partial collapse at the sinus entry keeps upstream venous pressure just above ICP, coupling the two.

advancedTest.q: A surgeon plans a dominant-side subtemporal approach. Sacrificing which vein risks temporal venous infarction and aphasia?
advancedTest.explain: The vein of Labbé drains the lateral temporal lobe into the transverse sinus.

advancedTest.q: A neonate with high-output heart failure and a large midline venous structure behind the third ventricle most likely has:
advancedTest.explain: Arteriovenous shunting into the median prosencephalic vein causes heart failure in newborns.

advancedTest.q: Why is resecting a developmental venous anomaly usually avoided?
choices: It drains normal brain, so removal causes venous infarction
advancedTest.explain: A DVA is the venous drainage of normal tissue; removing it can infarct that tissue.

lessons.title: The Blood–Brain Barrier

levels.kid:
Your brain is like a castle with a very careful guard at the gate.

The walls of the tiny blood pipes in your brain are squeezed super tight together, so most things in the blood can't sneak through. This wall is called the blood–brain barrier.

The guard lets in good things the brain needs, like sugar for energy. It keeps out many germs and things that could hurt the brain.

But the guard is so careful that it also keeps out lots of medicines! That makes it tricky for doctors to treat brain sicknesses. Scientists are inventing clever ways to sneak good medicine past the guard.

A few tiny spots of the brain have no wall, so the brain can taste the blood and check what's in it.
levels.hs:
The **blood–brain barrier (BBB)** is a protective wall between the blood and brain tissue. It keeps the brain's chemical environment stable and blocks many toxins, germs and drugs.

**What makes the barrier?**
- **Endothelial cells** of brain capillaries are sealed together by **tight junctions**, so substances can't slip between cells.
- Brain capillaries have **no small pores (fenestrations)**, unlike capillaries in muscles or the gut.
- **Pericytes** and the end-feet of **astrocytes** wrap around the vessels and help maintain the barrier.

**What gets through?**
- Small, **fat-soluble (lipophilic)** molecules like oxygen, carbon dioxide, alcohol and many anesthetics diffuse across.
- Essential nutrients get special **transporters**: glucose uses **GLUT1**, and some amino acids have their own carriers.
- **Efflux pumps** actively push many drugs back into the blood.

**Where is there no barrier?** A few small areas called **circumventricular organs** need to sense or release substances into the blood, such as the **area postrema** (which triggers vomiting when it detects toxins) and the **posterior pituitary** (which releases hormones).

**Why it matters in medicine:**
- Many drugs can't reach brain tumors or infections.
- **Parkinson's disease**: dopamine itself can't cross, so patients take **L-DOPA**, which crosses and is converted into dopamine in the brain.
- When the barrier breaks down (tumors, infections, MS), contrast dye leaks into brain tissue and lights up on MRI.
levels.college:
**The neurovascular unit**: endothelial cells, basement membrane, **pericytes**, **astrocyte end-feet** (rich in **aquaporin-4**), microglia and neurons, acting together to regulate the barrier and blood flow.

**Barrier properties of brain endothelium:**
- **Tight junctions** made of claudin-5, occludin and junctional adhesion molecules, anchored by ZO-1.
- No fenestrations and very little **transcytosis** (suppressed by MFSD2A).
- **Efflux transporters** on the luminal membrane: **P-glycoprotein (ABCB1)** and **BCRP (ABCG2)** pump many lipophilic drugs back out.
- **Carrier-mediated transport**: **GLUT1** (glucose), **LAT1** (large neutral amino acids, including L-DOPA), **MCT1** (lactate, ketones).
- **Receptor-mediated transcytosis**: transferrin and insulin receptors move large proteins.

**Passive permeability** favors small (roughly under 400–500 Da), lipophilic, uncharged molecules with few hydrogen bonds.

**Circumventricular organs** (fenestrated capillaries): **area postrema** (chemoreceptor trigger zone), **OVLT** and **subfornical organ** (osmolality and angiotensin sensing, thirst and vasopressin), **median eminence**, **posterior pituitary** and **pineal gland**. The **blood–CSF barrier** is at the **choroid plexus epithelium**, whose capillaries are fenestrated but whose epithelial cells have tight junctions.

**Pharmacology examples:** **carbidopa** does not cross the BBB, so it blocks peripheral L-DOPA decarboxylation without blocking it in the brain. Second-generation antihistamines are less sedating partly because they are P-gp substrates and less lipophilic. **Loperamide** is an opioid kept out of the CNS by P-gp. Inflamed meninges increase penicillin penetration.

**Barrier breakdown** → **vasogenic edema** (plasma leaks into extracellular space, white matter predominant, responds to steroids in tumors) versus **cytotoxic edema** (cell swelling from energy failure, as in early ischemic stroke, involves gray and white matter, restricted diffusion on MRI). **Neonatal kernicterus**: unconjugated bilirubin enters the immature brain and damages the basal ganglia.
levels.phd:
**Induction and maintenance.** BBB properties are not intrinsic to endothelium; they are induced by the neural environment. **Wnt/β-catenin signaling** (Wnt7a/b via GPR124 and RECK) drives CNS angiogenesis and barrier genes. **Pericytes** suppress transcytosis and leukocyte adhesion molecules; pericyte-deficient mice have a leaky BBB with intact tight junctions, showing transcytosis is a major leak route. **MFSD2A**, a lysophosphatidylcholine (DHA) transporter, enriches endothelial membranes in DHA, which inhibits caveolae formation and suppresses transcytosis. Astrocytes contribute Sonic hedgehog signaling and polarized AQP4 but are not required to initiate barrier formation.

**BBB dysfunction in disease.** Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI shows subtle leakage in aging and early cognitive decline, especially in the hippocampus, correlating with pericyte injury markers (soluble PDGFRβ) independent of amyloid and tau in some cohorts. **APOE4** accelerates BBB breakdown via a cyclophilin A–MMP9 pathway in pericytes. In MS, leukocytes cross via adhesion molecules (VLA-4 binding VCAM-1), the target of natalizumab. In glioblastoma, the barrier is disrupted in the enhancing core but intact in the infiltrative margin, where tumor cells evade drugs that cannot cross.

**Drug delivery strategies:**
- **Medicinal chemistry**: lowering polar surface area, hydrogen bond donors and P-gp liability (CNS MPO scores).
- **Receptor-mediated transcytosis**: bispecific antibodies against the transferrin receptor ("brain shuttles"), with an approved enzyme-replacement example in Japan for Hunter syndrome.
- **Osmotic disruption** with intra-arterial hyperosmolar mannitol.
- **MR-guided focused ultrasound** with intravenous microbubbles opens the BBB transiently and focally, being trialed to enhance antibody and chemotherapy delivery.
- **Bypass**: intrathecal or intraventricular dosing (as with antisense oligonucleotides like nusinersen), **convection-enhanced delivery**, and local implants.

The BBB is also an immune interface: brain endothelium carries signals from systemic inflammation into the CNS via cytokine receptors and prostaglandin synthesis.
levels.expert:
**Reading edema on imaging.** Vasogenic edema spreads along white matter in finger-like projections, sparing cortex, around tumors, abscesses and contusions; it improves with corticosteroids in tumors (not in trauma, where steroids increase mortality, per CRASH). Cytotoxic edema appears within minutes of ischemia as restricted diffusion on DWI, involves gray matter and does not respond to steroids. **Interstitial edema** is transependymal CSF seepage in acute hydrocephalus. Knowing which you are seeing changes management.

**Contrast enhancement means barrier breakdown**, not necessarily tumor: ring enhancement has a differential (glioblastoma, metastasis, abscess, demyelination often with an incomplete ring, resolving hematoma, radiation necrosis). Abscesses usually show central restricted diffusion. Post-radiation pseudoprogression mimics tumor growth in the months after chemoradiation, so do not rush to call progression.

**Surgery and the barrier.** **5-ALA** fluorescence-guided resection exploits tumor metabolism and barrier disruption to show high-grade glioma margins in the operating room. Carmustine wafers deliver chemotherapy directly to the resection bed, bypassing the BBB. **Laser interstitial thermal therapy** (LITT) for deep lesions can transiently open the barrier around the ablation zone, a period being studied for drug delivery.

**Pharmacology at the bedside.**
- Antibiotics for CNS infection must penetrate: choose agents with good CSF penetration and recognize that penetration falls as meningeal inflammation resolves.
- P-gp inhibitors can increase CNS exposure to substrate drugs, causing unexpected toxicity.
- Many anticancer antibodies and targeted drugs fail in brain metastases because of the barrier, so CNS-penetrant agents (for example certain EGFR and ALK inhibitors in lung cancer) changed management of brain metastases.
- **Osmotic agents** (mannitol, hypertonic saline) depend on an intact barrier to pull water from brain; where the barrier is broken, they may leak in and draw less water.

**Hyperosmolar disorders**: rapid sodium correction can cause **osmotic demyelination** in the pons, partly via glial apoptosis and barrier disruption.

keyPoints: BBB = brain capillary endothelium with tight junctions, no fenestrations, little transcytosis, plus pericytes and astrocyte end-feet.
Small lipophilic molecules diffuse across; glucose uses GLUT1, L-DOPA uses LAT1; P-glycoprotein pumps many drugs out.
Circumventricular organs lack a BBB: area postrema, OVLT, subfornical organ, median eminence, posterior pituitary, pineal.
Dopamine can't cross; L-DOPA can. Carbidopa stays outside the brain.
Barrier breakdown → vasogenic edema and contrast enhancement; ischemia → cytotoxic edema.
Delivery strategies: chemistry, transcytosis shuttles, osmotic opening, focused ultrasound, intrathecal and local delivery.

examples.src: A brain tumor lights up with contrast on MRI and is surrounded by finger-like white matter swelling.
examples.tr: Barrier breakdown in the tumor with vasogenic edema, which often responds to steroids.

examples.src: Why does chemotherapy struggle against cancer cells at the edge of a glioblastoma?
examples.tr: The barrier is still intact in the infiltrative margin, so many drugs can't reach those cells.

test.q: What mainly seals brain capillary endothelial cells together?
test.explain: Tight junctions (claudin-5, occludin) block the gaps between endothelial cells.

test.q: Which molecule crosses the BBB most easily by simple diffusion?
test.explain: Small, fat-soluble, uncharged molecules diffuse through membranes.

test.q: Glucose crosses the BBB using:
test.explain: GLUT1 is the main glucose transporter of brain endothelium.

test.q: Which area lacks a BBB and triggers vomiting in response to toxins?
test.explain: The area postrema is a circumventricular organ containing the chemoreceptor trigger zone.

test.q: Why is L-DOPA given in Parkinson's disease instead of dopamine?
choices: Dopamine can't cross the BBB, but L-DOPA can
test.explain: L-DOPA uses the LAT1 amino acid transporter, then is converted to dopamine in the brain.

test.q: Carbidopa is combined with L-DOPA because carbidopa:
choices: Blocks peripheral conversion of L-DOPA and does not cross the BBB
Crosses into the brain and makes more dopamine
test.explain: It inhibits peripheral decarboxylase, so more L-DOPA reaches the brain and peripheral side effects drop.

test.q: P-glycoprotein at the BBB:
choices: Pumps many drugs back into the blood
test.explain: P-gp is an efflux transporter limiting CNS entry of many drugs.

test.q: Which cells wrap brain capillaries with end-feet?
test.explain: Astrocyte end-feet, rich in aquaporin-4, cover most of the capillary surface.

test.q: Contrast enhancement of a lesion on MRI usually means:
choices: The lesion is always a tumor
The BBB is broken down there
test.explain: Gadolinium normally stays in vessels; enhancement means it leaked across a disrupted barrier.

test.q: Cytotoxic edema is typical of:
test.explain: Energy failure causes cells to swell; DWI shows restricted diffusion.

test.q: Name the barrier at the choroid plexus (blood–___ barrier).
test.explain: The blood–CSF barrier is formed by choroid plexus epithelial tight junctions.

test.q: Edema from leaky vessels around a tumor is called ___ edema.
test.explain: Vasogenic edema follows white matter tracts and often responds to steroids in tumors.

test.q: Unconjugated bilirubin crossing an immature BBB in newborns causes ___.
test.explain: Kernicterus damages the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei.

kidTest.q: The blood–brain barrier is like a:
choices: Careful guard at a castle gate
kidTest.explain: It carefully decides what gets into the brain.

kidTest.q: What good thing does the guard let in?
kidTest.explain: Sugar (glucose) gets a special door.

kidTest.q: Why is the barrier tricky for doctors?
choices: It keeps out lots of medicines too
kidTest.explain: Many medicines can't get past it.

kidTest.q: What keeps the pipe walls so tight?
choices: The wall cells are squeezed super close together
kidTest.explain: Tight junctions hold the cells closely together.

kidTest.q: The guard wall is called the blood–brain ___.
kidTest.explain: It's the blood–brain barrier.

advancedTest.q: Pericyte-deficient mice have a leaky BBB despite intact tight junctions. This shows that a major leak route is:
advancedTest.explain: Pericytes suppress endothelial transcytosis; without them vesicular transport rises.

advancedTest.q: Why do steroids help peritumoral edema but are avoided in traumatic brain injury?
choices: They reduce vasogenic edema in tumors, but the CRASH trial showed increased mortality in TBI
advancedTest.explain: Tumor edema is vasogenic and steroid-responsive; CRASH found higher mortality with steroids after head injury.

advancedTest.q: MFSD2A suppresses transcytosis at the BBB by:
choices: Enriching membranes in DHA, which inhibits caveolae formation
advancedTest.explain: Its DHA transport changes membrane lipid composition and reduces caveolar vesicles.

advancedTest.q: A new drug for brain metastases fails despite strong activity elsewhere. The most likely pharmacological reason is:
choices: It crosses the BBB too well
It is a P-glycoprotein substrate with poor CNS penetration
advancedTest.explain: Efflux by P-gp/BCRP is a classic reason for poor CNS exposure.
